summary: In HTTP/1.1 a client may ask to change protocols on an existing connection. This document discusses security issues with data the client sends before the change is confirmed, and adds requirements to RFC 9112 and RFC 9298.

eli5.summary: Don't start talking in a new language before the other side agrees to it, because they may understand something different.

questions: what is optimistic protocol transition in http
why must proxies close the connection after a rejected connect
can a client send data before an upgrade is accepted
subtitle: Why a client must not send data in a new protocol before the server has agreed to switch, and what proxies must do about it.

tldr.problem: In HTTP/1.1 a client can ask to switch protocols on an open connection. If it starts speaking the new protocol before the server answers, the server may read that data as ordinary HTTP requests.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC explains the request smuggling and parser risks, reviews existing upgrade tokens, and adds a rule for HTTP CONNECT: wait for a 2xx response or send Connection: close, and proxy servers must close the connection when they reject a CONNECT.
tldr.outcome: It updates RFC 9112 and RFC 9298 so HTTP/1.1 clients and proxies close this hole, and it gives future upgrade tokens guidance on avoiding it.

today: RFC 9931 is a Proposed Standard published in March 2026. It updates RFC 9112 and RFC 9298, and no later RFC is listed as updating or obsoleting it.

sections.title: What This Document Covers
sections.content:
This RFC discusses security considerations that arise when switching from HTTP/1.1 to a different protocol on the same connection. It reviews the relevant standards, discusses the risks if a client sends data before the transition is confirmed, evaluates existing upgrade tokens, and gives guidance for implementations and future standards.

It also changes two other specifications. New normative requirements for HTTP/1.1 are in its Section 8, and a replacement for a paragraph of RFC 9298 is in Section 6.3.
sections.eli5: This paper explains a trap in the way computers agree to switch to a new way of talking, and it adds rules to avoid falling in.

sections.title: How HTTP/1.1 Switches Protocols
sections.content:
In HTTP/1.1 requests are strictly sequential, and each new request is told apart implicitly by the end of the previous one. HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 instead label each request with an explicit stream ID. HTTP/1.1 is also the only HTTP version that lets a client change the protocol for the rest of the connection.

There are two mechanisms. The Upgrade header field says the client would like to use the connection for another protocol, and the server accepts with a 101 (Switching Protocols) status. The CONNECT method asks for a TCP connection to a host and port, and a 2xx response turns the connection into a TCP tunnel.

Both can be rejected, for reasons such as an unsupported token, a required authentication, a moved resource, an unreachable destination or a policy that forbids it. After a rejection the server keeps reading the connection as HTTP/1.1.

A client cannot switch in the middle of a message, so finishing the request is necessary. It is not sufficient, because the server may still say no. A client that expects a yes, for example because the same token recently succeeded, may send the first bytes of the new protocol optimistically, without waiting for the answer. That saves delay and is the behavior this RFC examines.
sections.eli5: You ask a friend, "Can we switch to our secret code?" If you start using the code before they answer and they said no, they will read your code as normal words and get confused.

sections.title: The Two Attacks
sections.content:
With only a client and a server, a protocol change adds no new risk, since each side must already cope with arbitrary data from the other. The problem appears when a third party, such as a website or an application, controls some of the data. If that party is untrusted, the data is attacker-controlled.

Request smuggling (Section 4.1). If the server accepts the switch it reads the following bytes in the new protocol. If it rejects the switch it reads them as HTTP/1.1. The client cannot know which until it sees the status code. An attacker who can place bytes in the new protocol stream can therefore make the server see an extra HTTP request that appears to come from the client. The example in the RFC is a proxy client authenticated by a TLS client certificate. A malicious application asks for a connection to a nonexistent destination and sends a valid POST request for the proxy itself. The proxy answers the failed CONNECT with 504 and then treats the smuggled POST as authenticated.

Parser exploits (Section 4.2). If the server trusts its HTTP client and assumes request data is not attacker-controlled, optimistic sending can break that assumption and expose bugs in the server's request parser.
sections.eli5: It is like a hall pass. If a stranger slips a note into your pile of homework and the teacher reads it as your note, the stranger has borrowed your good name.

sections.title: Existing Upgrade Tokens
sections.content:
The RFC checks the registered upgrade tokens it believes are in use.

  • TLS (RFC 2817): optimistic TLS data cannot be valid HTTP/1.1, because the first octet of a TLS connection must be 22 (handshake), which is not allowed in an HTTP/1.1 method. A compliant server treats it as a parsing error and closes the connection.
  • WebSocket (RFC 6455): the client MUST wait for the server response before sending more data, and client frames use high-entropy masking. Optimistic use is already forbidden.
  • connect-udp (RFC 9298): it allowed optimistic UDP packets, which is risky in HTTP/1.1. This RFC replaces that text so a client MAY do so only with HTTP/2 or later and MUST NOT send UDP packets optimistically in HTTP/1.x.
  • connect-ip (RFC 9484): it already forbids optimistic sending in HTTP/1.1.
sections.eli5: The authors checked each existing secret handshake. Most already say "wait for the yes", and the one that did not now does.

sections.title: Rules for HTTP CONNECT
sections.content:
This section updates RFC 9112 and applies only to HTTP/1.1. Proxy clients that send CONNECT on behalf of untrusted TCP clients MUST do one or both of these: wait for a 2xx response before forwarding any TCP payload data, or send a Connection: close request header. A client that does neither is open to a trivial request smuggling attack.

Because some clients are believed to be vulnerable today, proxy servers MUST close the underlying connection when they reject a CONNECT request, without processing further requests on it. This applies whether or not the request had a close connection option.

The mitigation often slows connection setup for correct clients, especially with a 407 response. HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 are not vulnerable and avoid that cost. A proxy server MAY turn the mitigation off for a client known to wait for a 2xx, which it can identify with the User-Agent header and the vendor's documentation.
sections.eli5: Wait for the green light before you push your cart through, or promise to leave afterwards. And a shopkeeper who says no should close the door so nobody sneaks in behind.

sections.title: Why Not Always Close the Connection
sections.content:
When a server rejects a transition, the connection can normally carry on as HTTP/1.1. There is no general requirement to close it, and keeping it open has performance advantages if more requests to that server are likely, so closing is normally inappropriate.

The CONNECT rule above is a deliberate exception, adopted as a mitigation for clients believed to be vulnerable.
sections.eli5: Normally you keep the phone line open for the next question. Closing it only makes sense when you suspect someone is listening in.

sections.title: Guidance for Future Upgrade Tokens
sections.content:
The RFC lists designs that reduce or remove the risk and may suit future specifications: forbid optimistic use of Upgrade (as WebSocket and connect-ip do), embed a fixed preamble that deliberately ends HTTP/1.1 processing (as RFC 9113 does), or apply high-entropy masking of client-to-server data (as WebSocket does). Future token specifications should account for these issues and say how implementations avoid them.

It also advises restricting new tokens to GET requests with no content when the method is otherwise irrelevant and no message content is needed. That matches the existing tokens other than TLS and simplifies servers.
sections.eli5: When people invent new secret handshakes, they should copy the safe ones: wait for the yes, start with a clear signal, or scramble the message.
